sections.title: 1. Purpose and place in the outline

blocks.text: Grade 3 is the chemistry year of the four-year cycle (§4): matter, its states, and simple reactions. The outline is clear that grammar-stage science is observation, classification and nature study, not premature theory (§3D). So this course is built on doing and looking: kitchen-table demonstrations, careful observation, naming and sorting, and a written record of what was seen. Atoms and molecules are named, not explained; the explaining comes in the logic stage.
Every student also keeps a nature journal from Grade 1: sketch, label, date, describe (§3D). It continues every week this year, alongside the chemistry.

head: Task
What the student does
Time

A hands-on experiment with kitchen materials, done with a parent
A page recording the demonstration: the question, what we did, what we saw (in words and a drawing), and the week's new words

blocks.text: Order within the week: A before B; C after B, while it's fresh. D any time, ideally outdoors on a day with good weather.
36 weeks in 6 six-week terms.
4 tasks a week, so 24 per term, all in the weekly queue.
Expected time: about 1½–2 hours a week. A family may run all four tasks in one long session (§7 gives that example for science exactly).

Teacher's source: The Secret of Everyday Things by Jean-Henri Fabre (English translation 1920, public domain). Fabre, the great French naturalist, explains the chemistry of the household, such as salt, soap, fire, air and water, in a warm conversational style. The parent reads the relevant chapter beforehand and retells or reads parts aloud. It's read as Fabre wrote it.

Child's readers: the Let's-Read-and-Find-Out Science series, Level 2, for example What Is the World Made Of? (Kathleen Weidner Zoehfeld) and Air Is All Around You (Franklyn M. Branley). They're short picture books the child can read alone.

Terms 5–6 read-aloud: The Mystery of the Periodic Table by Benjamin D. Wiker, a living book telling the story of the chemists, from the ancients to the elements. Read the early chapters only; the rest waits for later grades.
Each term manual names the readings for each week.

head: Term
Topic
What the child does and learns
rows: What matter is: it takes up space and has weight. Describing materials by color, shape, hardness, texture; weighing on a balance; sink or float; magnetic or not; sorting materials (wood, metal, glass, stone, cloth)
The three states; air is matter; melting and freezing; evaporation and condensation; the water cycle; candle wax melting and hardening
Mixing and separating (sieving, filtering, magnets, evaporation); dissolving sugar and salt; what speeds dissolving; growing salt and sugar crystals

Physical changes (cutting, melting, dissolving) versus chemical changes (something new is made); the signs of a chemical change (bubbles, color, heat, smell); baking soda and vinegar; rust; a burning candle; changes in cooking
Everyday chemistry: acids, bases, salt and soap
Red cabbage indicator; acids and bases in the kitchen; how salt is made from seawater; how soap is made and how it cleans; natural dyes
Elements as the simplest kinds of matter (gold, iron, copper, carbon, oxygen); ten common elements and their symbols; the stories of Robert Boyle, Antoine Lavoisier and John Dalton; year review

blocks.text: Why this order. Each term builds on the one before. You can't see that a change is chemical (Term 4) without knowing the states (Term 2) and mixtures (Term 3). And the elements (Term 6) are where the year's questions lead: what is everything made of?
Every week, all year, one outdoor observation: a leaf, a bird, a cloud, frost on a window, rust on a gate.
The page has four things: a sketch, labels, the date and place, and two or three sentences describing it.
Chemistry connections are welcome but not required: frost and dew (Term 2), puddles drying (Term 3), rust and rotting leaves (Term 4).
The journal follows the seasons, so each term manual suggests what to look for at that time of year.
The nature journal is part of the portfolio and carries forward through Grade 12 (§5, Grade 1).
Every demonstration uses kitchen materials (water, salt, sugar, baking soda, vinegar, food coloring, candles, red cabbage) and is done with a parent present.
Heat and flame (melting wax, boiling water, a burning candle) are handled by the parent; the child watches from a safe distance and records.
Nothing is tasted unless the manual says it's a food and safe to taste.
Safety goggles are a good habit to start this year, even when they aren't strictly needed.
Narration (task A): oral, not graded.
Lab notebook (task C): checked each week for the three parts: the question, what we did, what we saw. Not graded; the parent notes whether all three are there.
Science words go into the Memory Work queue (11): the three states, the names of the changes (melting, freezing, evaporating, condensing, dissolving), and in Term 6, ten elements and their symbols.

Term check (week 6 of each term): a short written check, about 10 items: naming, sorting, matching words to meanings, and describing one demonstration in two or three sentences. 8 of 10 is the term standard; written assessment begins in Grade 3 (§8). Below that, the next term opens by reviewing the missed ideas.
Year-end: the child explains, with a demonstration of their choice, one thing they learned this year, to the family or co-op.

head: Course
Link
rows: Weighing and measuring: Term 4's weight and capacity lessons come just in time for Term 4's measured experiments

Colonial candle-dipping and onion-skin dyeing (History Term 2) are early chemistry, revisited in Science Terms 2 and 5; Lewis and Clark's salt-making at the Pacific (History Term 5) pairs with Science Term 5
The three states, the names of the changes, ten elements and symbols
The Hearth's Grade 3 food preservation by freezing and drying (§6) uses Term 2's freezing and Term 3's evaporation; cooking shows chemical change (Term 4)

blocks.text: Content work carries over freely (§7). A missed week moves the sequence later; the term's review week absorbs one.
Demonstrations can be bunched. A family may do two in one Saturday session and skip a week. The lab notebook still gets a page for each.
The nature journal shouldn't be skipped for long. Bad weather can be observed through a window.

sections.title: 10. What each term manual will contain

blocks.text: For each week: the reading, a narration prompt, the demonstration (materials, steps, what to watch for, and the safety note), the lab notebook prompt and the week's new words, and a nature journal suggestion. For each term: a materials list, and the term check with its answer key.

terms.title: Matter and Its Properties

head: Big idea
Everything around us is matter: it takes up space and has weight. We can describe matter by its properties, and sort it by them.
rows: What matter is · describing properties · weighing on a balance · sink or float · magnetic or not · sorting materials and review
What Is the World Made Of? (Zoehfeld) · What Makes a Magnet? (Branley) · Fabre, The Secret of Everyday Things, for the parent
Early autumn. Choose one "year tree" near home to draw once each term

glance.text: How each week works. A: read and narrate. B: the demonstration, with a parent. C: the lab notebook page, right after B. D: the nature journal, outdoors. Every lab notebook page has three parts: the question, what we did, what we saw (words and a drawing), plus the week's new words.
Safety. Kitchen materials only, a parent present for every demonstration, nothing tasted.

blocks.text: Balloons · a clear bowl or sink of water · paper towels · a sewing needle or nail, a penny and a few stones (for scratch tests) · a coat hanger, string and two paper cups (for a homemade balance) · aluminum foil · modeling clay · ten small household objects (a spoon, a cork, a key, a crayon, a marble, an eraser, a button, a coin, a leaf, a bottle cap) · a magnet · paper clips · a cloth bag
What Is the World Made Of?, the opening pages. Narrate: "What is matter? Name five things in this room that are matter."

Is air matter? (1) Push an "empty" cup straight down, upside down, into a bowl of water, with a dry paper towel stuffed in the bottom. Lift it out: the towel is dry, because air filled the cup and kept the water out. (2) Tie an empty balloon and a full balloon to the two ends of a stick hung from a string at its middle: the full balloon side dips. Air takes up space and has weight.
Question: Is air matter? Draw the cup in the bowl. New words: matter · weight · space
Choose the year tree. Draw the whole tree; label the trunk, branches and leaves; write the date and the color of the leaves today.

Parent reads a short passage from Fabre's opening chapters on the things of the household, or explains: everything has properties — what it looks like, feels like, how hard it is. Narrate: "What are some ways to describe a stone?"

Mystery bag: put five objects in a cloth bag; the child reaches in and describes each by feel only (smooth, rough, soft, hard, cold) before guessing. Then a scratch test: try to scratch a stone, a piece of wood, a crayon and a piece of chalk with a fingernail, then a penny, then a nail (parent holds the nail). Which are hardest?
Question: Which things are hardest? Make a table: object / scratched by fingernail? / by penny? / by nail? New words: property · texture · hard · soft
Find three different stones. Draw them, and describe each one's color, texture and hardness.
Parent explains: a balance compares weights. The heavier side goes down. Big doesn't always mean heavy. Narrate: "How does a balance tell which thing is heavier?"

Make a balance: hang two paper cups from the ends of a coat hanger with string, and hang the hanger from a doorknob. Compare pairs: a marble and a cork; a crayon and a key. Then make a ball of foil and a ball of clay the same size, and weigh them against each other.
Question: Are things the same size always the same weight? Draw the balance with the foil and clay balls. New words: balance · heavier · lighter
Collect two different seeds or nuts (an acorn, a maple seed, a pinecone). Draw them and weigh them on the balance.
Parent explains: some things float and some sink, and shape can change which. Narrate: "Did anything surprise you today?" (after B)

Predict, then test: list the ten household objects; the child predicts sink or float for each, then tests them in a bowl of water. Then: a sheet of foil crumpled into a tight ball sinks; the same foil shaped into a boat floats. Finally, a lump of clay sinks; shaped into a boat, it floats and can carry a few paper clips.
Question: Can shape change whether something floats? Table: object / prediction / result. New words: float · sink · predict
Drop a few leaves and twigs on a puddle or stream. Do they float? Draw them on the water.
What Makes a Magnet? Narrate: "What kinds of things does a magnet pull?"

Magnet hunt: predict, then test which of the household objects a magnet attracts. Only things made of iron or steel are attracted; a copper-colored penny, foil and most coins are not. Then: does a magnet pull a paper clip through a sheet of paper? Through your hand? Through water in a cup?
Question: What does a magnet attract? Two lists: attracted / not attracted. New words: magnet · attract · iron
Watch and draw one bird. Label its beak, wings, tail and feet.

weeks.title: Sorting materials; review and term check

blocks.text: The child reads back the term's five lab notebook pages and tells about the favorite demonstration.

Sorting materials: gather twenty things from around the house and sort them by what they're made of: wood, metal, glass, plastic, stone, cloth. Then sort the same things a different way: hard or soft, heavy or light, magnetic or not. One pile, many ways to sort.
Below. Written, about 15 minutes.
Draw the year tree again, and compare it with week 1. What has changed?
1. What two things are true of all matter?
2. Is air matter? How do you know?
3. Name three properties you could use to describe a stone.
4. What tool compares the weights of two things?
5. A ball of foil sinks, but the same foil shaped like a boat floats. What changed?
6. Magnets attract things made of ___ or steel.
7. Will a magnet pick up a piece of aluminum foil?
8. Sort these by material: a spoon, a window, a table. (metal, glass, wood)
9. What word means "how something feels when you touch it"?
10. Describe one demonstration from this term in 2–3 sentences.

1. It takes up space and it has weight. · 2. Yes; for example, the paper towel stayed dry, or the full balloon was heavier. · 3. Any three: color, shape, size, texture, hardness, weight. · 4. A balance. · 5. Its shape. · 6. Iron. · 7. No. · 8. Spoon: metal; window: glass; table: wood. · 9. Texture. · 10. Any clear description with what was done and what was seen.
Standard: 8 of 10. Below that, review the missed ideas at the start of Term 2.
Prediction comes first. Always ask "What do you think will happen?" before a demonstration, and write the guess down. Being wrong is the most interesting part.
Let the child do the hands-on parts. The parent reads, sets up and keeps it safe; the child pours, weighs, tests and records.
The year tree gives the nature journal a thread through the seasons. Draw it once each term.
Gather the term's materials before week 1
Set up the lab notebook (any blank or graph-paper notebook) and the nature journal
Add the term's science words to the Memory Work queue
Week 6: give the term check and record the score

terms.mastery: Standard: 8 of 10. Below that, review the missed ideas at the start of Term 2.

terms.title: Solids, Liquids and Gases

head: Big idea
Matter comes in three states: solid, liquid and gas. Heating and cooling can change one into another.
rows: The three states · air is a gas · melting and freezing · candle wax · evaporation and condensation · the water cycle and review
What Is the World Made Of? (reread) · Air Is All Around You (Branley) · Down Comes the Rain (Branley) · Fabre, The Secret of Everyday Things, the chapters on water and air, for the parent
Late autumn: frost, dew, fog, clouds, and falling leaves

glance.text: How each week works. A: read and narrate. B: the demonstration, with a parent. C: the lab notebook page (the question, what we did, what we saw, new words). D: the nature journal.
Safety. The parent handles all hot water and melted wax. The child watches from a safe distance.

blocks.text: Clear cups and containers of different shapes · a measuring cup · balloons · an empty plastic bottle · two bowls (one of hot tap water, one of ice water) · ice cubes · a plastic cup and a marker · a candle stub or wax, and a small pan for melting (parent only) · a cloth · a glass · a pot lid · a zip-top bag and tape
What Is the World Made Of?, the pages on solids, liquids and gases. Narrate: "How is a solid different from a liquid?"

Pour one cup of water into three differently shaped containers in turn. The shape changes; the amount stays the same. Put a wooden block in each container: its shape doesn't change. Then blow up a balloon: the air spreads to fill whatever holds it.
Question: How do solids, liquids and gases behave? Draw one of each. New words: solid · liquid · gas · state
Find one solid, one liquid and one gas outdoors (a rock, a puddle, and wind or your breath on a cold day). Draw and label them.
Air Is All Around You. Narrate: "How do we know air is there, if we can't see it?"

Stretch a balloon over the mouth of an empty plastic bottle. Stand the bottle in a bowl of hot tap water (parent pours): the balloon puffs up as the air inside warms and spreads. Move it to ice water: the balloon shrinks.
Question: What happens to air when it's warmed and cooled? Draw the bottle in both bowls. New words: air · expand · shrink
On a windy day, draw what the wind is moving: trees, leaves, clouds, a flag.

intro.text: Hearth link: The Hearth's Grade 3 food preservation includes freezing (§6). Freezing a few berries this week makes the same point.

blocks.text: Fabre's chapter on water, or a parent explanation: a solid melts into a liquid when heated; a liquid freezes into a solid when cooled. Water freezes at 32 °F. Narrate: "What's the difference between melting and freezing?"

(1) Ice race: put ice cubes in three places (a sunny window, a shady room, the refrigerator) and check every 15 minutes. Which melts first? (2) Fill a plastic cup half full of water, mark the level, and freeze it overnight. The ice is higher than the mark: water grows when it freezes.
Question: Where does ice melt fastest? Record the times. New words: melt · freeze
Look for frost on grass, windows or car roofs on a cold morning. Draw it, and note the time it melted away.

Fabre's chapter on the candle, or a parent explanation. History's week 8 candle-dipping showed wax changing state; now look closely. Narrate: "What happens to wax when it's heated, and when it cools?"

Parent only: melt a little wax in a small pan over low heat. The child watches it turn from solid to liquid. Pour a little onto a foil plate and watch it turn back to solid as it cools. Then light a candle (parent) and watch the pool of liquid wax around the wick.
Question: Can wax change state and change back? Draw the solid wax, the melted wax and the hardened wax. New words: heat · cool · solid to liquid
Draw the year tree's falling leaves. Collect and press three of them in a heavy book.
Down Comes the Rain. Narrate: "Where does a puddle go when it dries up?"

(1) Hang a wet cloth to dry, and check it each hour: the water evaporates into the air as water vapor. (2) Fill a glass with ice water and watch drops form on the outside: water vapor from the air condenses on the cold glass. (3) Parent holds a cold pot lid over a pot of steaming water: drops form underneath and fall like rain.
Question: Where does water go, and how does it come back? Draw the cold glass with its drops. New words: evaporate · condense · water vapor
Look for dew on grass early in the morning, or fog. Draw it and write the time.

weeks.title: The water cycle; review and term check

blocks.text: The child reads back the term's lab notebook pages and draws the water cycle: the sun warms water, it evaporates; vapor rises and condenses into clouds; rain or snow falls; it gathers in rivers and seas, and the cycle repeats.
Water cycle in a bag: put a little water in a zip-top bag, seal it, and tape it to a sunny window. Over a few days, watch drops form at the top and run back down.
Below. Written, about 15 minutes.
Draw the sky: clouds, sun or rain. Label the kind of weather.
1–3. Name the state of each: a rock · orange juice · steam
4. Which state takes the shape of its container but keeps the same amount?
5. Ice turning into water is called ___.
6. Water turning into ice is called ___.
7. A puddle drying up in the sun is called ___.
8. Drops forming on the outside of a cold glass is called ___.
9. Put the water cycle in order: rain falls · water evaporates · clouds form
10. Describe one demonstration from this term in 2–3 sentences.

1. Solid · 2. Liquid · 3. Gas · 4. Liquid · 5. Melting · 6. Freezing · 7. Evaporation · 8. Condensation · 9. Water evaporates, clouds form, rain falls · 10. Any clear description with what was done and what was seen.
Standard: 8 of 10. Below that, review the missed ideas at the start of Term 3.
This term's words are memory work. Melt, freeze, evaporate, condense: add them to the Memory Work queue with a one-line meaning each.
Use the weather. Frost, fog and dew are free demonstrations. Point them out whenever they happen.
History links up in week 10. If the family dipped candles in History week 8, bring a candle to the table and remind the child what they made.
Gather the term's materials before week 7
Freeze the marked cup on the evening of week 9's Day 1
Add the term's science words to the Memory Work queue
Week 12: give the term check and record the score

terms.mastery: Standard: 8 of 10. Below that, review the missed ideas at the start of Term 3.

terms.title: Mixtures and Solutions

head: Big idea
Different kinds of matter can be mixed and then separated again. Some things dissolve in water to make a solution.
rows: Mixtures · filtering · separating with magnets and evaporation · dissolving · faster dissolving and growing crystals · review
Fabre, The Secret of Everyday Things, the chapters on water and salt, for the parent; parent explanations each week
Winter: snowflakes, ice, bare branches, evergreens, winter birds

glance.text: How each week works. A: read and narrate. B: the demonstration, with a parent. C: the lab notebook page (the question, what we did, what we saw, new words). D: the nature journal.
Safety. The parent handles all hot water. Iron-fortified cereal is a food, but once crushed and stirred for week 15, don't eat it.

blocks.text: Trail mix (or nuts, raisins and cereal) · sand and small gravel · a kitchen sieve · coffee filters and a funnel · clear cups · iron-fortified breakfast cereal, a zip-top bag and a strong magnet · salt · sugar · a dark plate · sugar cubes · hot and cold tap water · a spoon · a pencil, cotton string and a clean glass jar (for crystals) · a magnifying glass · black cloth or paper
Parent explains: a mixture is two or more things mixed together, where each keeps its own properties. Trail mix, salad and sand-and-gravel are mixtures. Narrate: "What makes something a mixture?"
(1) Mix a bowl of trail mix, then separate it by hand into its parts. (2) Mix sand and small gravel, then separate it with a sieve: the sand falls through, the gravel stays.
Question: Can a mixture be separated again? Draw the sieve with gravel in it. New words: mixture · separate · sieve
Look closely at a handful of soil or a patch of ground. Soil is a mixture: what can you find in it? (Bits of rock, leaves, roots, small creatures.)

Fabre's chapter on water, or a parent explanation: a filter lets water through but catches the bits mixed in it. Rivers and wells were often muddy; filters helped people get clean water. Narrate: "How does a filter work?"

Stir a spoonful of soil into a clear cup of water. Pour it through a coffee filter in a funnel into a second cup. The water comes through much clearer; the mud stays in the filter. (Don't drink the filtered water.)
Question: Can a filter clean muddy water? Draw the cup before and after. New words: filter · mud
Look at ice on a puddle or pond (from a safe place). Is it clear or cloudy? Draw it.

weeks.title: Separating with magnets and with evaporation

blocks.text: Parent explains: some mixtures can be separated by a property, such as being magnetic, or by letting the water evaporate away. Narrate: "Name two ways to separate a mixture."

(1) Iron in cereal: crush a cup of iron-fortified cereal in a zip-top bag, add water, and slosh it around. Hold a strong magnet against the bag, then tip the bag: tiny dark specks of iron gather at the magnet. (2) Salt from salt water: dissolve a spoonful of salt in a little warm water, pour it onto a dark plate, and set it in a sunny window. Over a few days the water evaporates and leaves the salt behind.
Question: How can we get the iron out of cereal, and the salt out of water? Draw both. New words: magnet · evaporate
If it snows, catch snowflakes on black cloth or paper and look at them with a magnifying glass. Draw one: each has six sides. If there's no snow, draw an evergreen branch.

Fabre's chapter on salt, or a parent explanation: some things dissolve in water, spreading through it until they can't be seen. The mixture is a solution. Some things don't dissolve at all. Narrate: "What happens when sugar dissolves?"

Fill three clear cups with water. Stir a spoonful of sugar into one, salt into another, and sand into the third. Which disappear? Which settles at the bottom? Taste a drop of the sugar water (it's food and safe): the sugar is still there, even though it can't be seen.
Question: What dissolves in water? Table: substance / dissolves? New words: dissolve · solution
Watch and draw a winter bird. Which birds stay all winter?

Parent explains: dissolving goes faster with warm water, stirring, and smaller pieces. And when a solution is left to dry slowly, the dissolved matter can come back as crystals. Narrate: "How can you make sugar dissolve faster?"

(1) Dissolving race: drop a sugar cube into cold water and another into warm water; time them. Then stir one and not another. Then compare a whole cube with a crushed one. (2) Grow crystals: the parent stirs as much salt as will dissolve into a cup of hot water. Pour it into a clean jar, hang a string from a pencil laid across the top, and leave it somewhere still. Check it each day for the next week.
Question: What makes sugar dissolve faster? Record the times. Then start a crystal diary: draw the string each day. New words: crystal · stir
Look for icicles. Draw one and describe how it formed.
The child reads back the term's lab notebook pages and shows the crystal string.
Look at the crystals with a magnifying glass. Salt crystals are tiny cubes. Compare them with grains of table salt under the glass: the same shape.
Below. Written, about 15 minutes.
Draw the year tree in winter, and compare it with Terms 1 and 2.
1. What is a mixture?
2. What would you use to separate gravel from sand?
3. What would you use to separate mud from water?
4. How could you get the iron out of crushed cereal?
5. How could you get the salt back out of salt water?
6. Does sugar dissolve in water?
7. Does sand dissolve in water?
8. Name two ways to make sugar dissolve faster.
9. Salt stirred into water until it disappears makes a ___.
10. Describe one demonstration from this term in 2–3 sentences.

1. Two or more things mixed together, each keeping its own properties · 2. A sieve · 3. A filter · 4. With a magnet · 5. Let the water evaporate · 6. Yes · 7. No · 8. Any two: warm water, stirring, crushing it into smaller pieces · 9. Solution · 10. Any clear description with what was done and what was seen.
Standard: 8 of 10. Below that, review the missed ideas at the start of Term 4.
Crystals take patience. They may take several days to appear. Keep the jar somewhere it won't be bumped.
Taste only the sugar water in week 16, and nothing else this term.
Snow is a gift. If it snows during the term, catch snowflakes whatever week it is. Six-sided crystals in the sky are this term's lesson in nature.
Gather the term's materials before week 13
Start the crystal jar in week 17 and check it daily into week 18
Add the term's science words to the Memory Work queue
Week 18: give the term check and record the score

terms.mastery: Standard: 8 of 10. Below that, review the missed ideas at the start of Term 4.

terms.title: Changes: Physical and Chemical

head: Big idea
Matter can change in two ways. In a physical change, it's still the same stuff (cut, melted or dissolved). In a chemical change, something new is made.
rows: Physical changes · chemical changes: baking soda and vinegar · the signs of a chemical change · rust · a measured reaction and a burning candle · cooking as chemistry, and review
Fabre, The Secret of Everyday Things, the chapters on fire, iron and bread, for the parent; parent explanations each week
Late winter: rust, rotting logs, the first buds, melting snow

glance.text: How each week works. A: read and narrate. B: the demonstration, with a parent. C: the lab notebook page (the question, what we did, what we saw, new words). D: the nature journal.
Safety. The parent lights and handles the candle in week 23 and does all stove work in week 24. Baking soda and vinegar are safe but messy: work on a tray.
Arithmetic link. Arithmetic's week 23 lesson teaches teaspoons, cups and ounces. This term's week 23 measured reaction uses them.

blocks.text: Paper and scissors · chocolate · baking soda · white vinegar · balloons and a small plastic bottle · a tray · an apple, a knife (parent) and lemon juice · milk · two clean jars, steel wool (soap-free) and water · measuring spoons · a candle, a clear glass jar and matches (parent only) · pancake ingredients

Parent explains: in a physical change, matter changes its shape, size or state, but it's still the same stuff. Cut paper is still paper; melted chocolate is still chocolate. Many physical changes can be undone. Narrate: "Is cut paper still paper?"

Make four physical changes and record each: (1) cut paper into pieces; (2) melt a square of chocolate in a warm hand, then let it harden in the refrigerator; (3) crumple foil, then flatten it; (4) dissolve sugar in water (it's still sugar; it could be evaporated back).
Question: Is it still the same stuff? Table: what we did / still the same stuff? / can it be undone? New words: physical change
Look for melting snow or ice, a physical change in nature. Draw it.

weeks.title: Chemical changes: baking soda and vinegar

blocks.text: Parent explains: in a chemical change, two things react and make something new that wasn't there before. Narrate: "What new thing was made when we mixed them?" (after B)

On a tray, put a spoonful of baking soda in a cup and pour in vinegar: it fizzes and bubbles. The bubbles are a new gas, called carbon dioxide. Then put two spoonfuls of baking soda inside a balloon, stretch the balloon over a bottle with a little vinegar in it, and lift the balloon so the baking soda drops in. The gas blows up the balloon.
Question: What happens when baking soda meets vinegar? Draw the balloon before and after. New words: chemical change · react · carbon dioxide
Look for the first buds on the year tree. Draw a twig with its buds.

weeks.title: The signs of a chemical change

blocks.text: Fabre's chapter on bread or on fire, or a parent explanation: we can tell a chemical change has happened by the signs: bubbles of gas, a new color, heat or light, or a new smell. Narrate: "Name the signs of a chemical change."

Look for the signs: (1) Color: cut an apple in half (parent cuts). Brush lemon juice on one half and leave the other plain. After an hour, the plain half has turned brown. (2) Smell: leave a spoonful of milk out on the counter for two days, then smell it: soured milk is a chemical change. (3) Bubbles: the baking soda from week 20.
Question: How can we tell a chemical change has happened? Draw the two apple halves. New words: sign · color · gas
Find a rotting log or a pile of old leaves. Rotting is a slow chemical change. Draw what you see.

Fabre's chapter on iron, or a parent explanation: rust is a chemical change. Iron, with water and air, slowly turns into rust, which is a new substance: reddish, crumbly and weak. Narrate: "What does iron need to rust?"

Put a pad of soap-free steel wool in each of two jars. Leave one dry. Wet the other and leave it open to the air. Check them every day for a week (into week 23): the wet one rusts; the dry one doesn't.
Question: What does iron need to rust? Rust diary: draw both jars each day. New words: rust · iron
Find something rusty outdoors: a gate, a nail, an old tool. Draw it and describe its color and texture.

weeks.title: A measured reaction and a burning candle

blocks.text: Fabre's chapter on fire, or a parent explanation: burning is a chemical change. Fire needs air to burn. Narrate: "Why did the candle go out?" (after B)

(1) Measured reaction: set up three bottles with the same amount of vinegar (half a cup each). Add 1, 2 and 3 teaspoons of baking soda in balloons, as in week 20. Which balloon grows biggest? (2) Parent only: light a candle on a plate, then carefully lower a clear glass jar over it. The flame shrinks and goes out when it has used up the part of the air it needs.
Question: Does more baking soda make more gas? Table: teaspoons / balloon size. Then draw the candle under the jar. New words: burn · flame · measure
Check the year tree's buds again. Have they opened?

weeks.title: Cooking as chemistry; review and term check

blocks.text: The child reads back the term's lab notebook pages and sorts the term's changes into physical and chemical.

Make pancakes (parent at the stove). Watch for chemical changes: bubbles rising in the batter from the baking powder, the surface changing color as it cooks, the smell. Could you turn a pancake back into batter? Hearth link: cooking is a Grade 3 practical-arts skill (§6).
Below. Written, about 15 minutes.
Draw something that changed outdoors this term: melted snow, rust, a bud opening.
Write physical or chemical:
1. Cutting paper · 2. Melting ice · 3. Burning wood · 4. Toasting bread
5. Name three signs of a chemical change.
6. What gas makes the bubbles when baking soda and vinegar mix?
7. What two things does iron need to rust?
8. Why does a candle go out under a jar?
9. Can you turn toast back into bread? What does that tell you about the change?
10. Describe one demonstration from this term in 2–3 sentences.

1. Physical · 2. Physical · 3. Chemical · 4. Chemical · 5. Any three: bubbles of gas, a new color, heat, light, a new smell · 6. Carbon dioxide · 7. Water and air · 8. It uses up the air it needs to burn · 9. No; it was a chemical change, and something new was made · 10. Any clear description with what was done and what was seen.
Standard: 8 of 10. Below that, review the missed ideas at the start of Term 5.
"Is it still the same stuff?" is the term's one question. Ask it about every change, in science and in the kitchen.
Start the rust jars on time. They need a week to show clear results, running into week 23.
Keep the candle demonstration in the parent's hands from lighting to blowing out. The child observes and records.
Gather the term's materials before week 19
Leave the milk out in week 21 and start the rust jars in week 22
Add "physical change, chemical change" and the signs to the Memory Work queue
Week 24: give the term check and record the score

terms.mastery: Standard: 8 of 10. Below that, review the missed ideas at the start of Term 5.

terms.title: Everyday Chemistry: Acids, Bases, Salt and Soap

head: Big idea
The kitchen and the washroom are full of chemistry: acids and bases, salt, soap and dyes.
rows: A red cabbage indicator · acids and bases at home · salt · soap · natural dyes · review
Fabre, The Secret of Everyday Things, the chapters on salt and soap, for the parent · The Mystery of the Periodic Table (Wiker), the opening chapters, read aloud
Spring: buds and blossoms, the colors of flowers, rain, the first insects

glance.text: How each week works. A: read and narrate. B: the demonstration, with a parent. C: the lab notebook page (the question, what we did, what we saw, new words). D: the nature journal.

The read-aloud begins this term. The Mystery of the Periodic Table tells the story of chemistry from the ancients onward. This term reads its opening chapters, on the earliest ideas about what things are made of. Term 6 continues with the chemists.
Safety. The parent boils the cabbage and the dye pots. Nothing is tasted this term except lemon juice in week 26.

blocks.text: Half a red cabbage, a pot and a strainer (parent) · clear cups · white vinegar · baking soda · lemon juice · milk · dish soap · a little toothpaste · salt and a magnifying glass · a bowl of water, ground pepper, cooking oil and a small jar with a lid · onion skins, beets or turmeric, and white cotton cloth (for dyeing)
The Mystery of the Periodic Table, the first chapter. Narrate: "What did the people of long ago think everything was made of?"

Parent: chop half a red cabbage, simmer it in water for 15 minutes, and strain out the purple juice. Let it cool. Pour a little into three clear cups. Add vinegar to one: it turns pink. Add baking soda water to another: it turns green or blue. Leave the third plain: it stays purple. The juice is an indicator: its color tells us what's been added.
Question: What does cabbage juice tell us? Color the three cups with colored pencils. New words: indicator · acid · base
Find and draw the first spring flower near home. What color is it?

The Mystery of the Periodic Table, continuing. Parent explains: acids taste sour (lemon, vinegar). Bases feel slippery (soap, baking soda). The cabbage juice turns pink for acids and green or blue for bases. Narrate: "Name two acids and two bases in our kitchen."

Test with the cabbage juice: lemon juice, milk, dish soap, a little toothpaste stirred into water, plain water. Sort them: acid, base or neither. Then pour vinegar into the green baking-soda cup a little at a time, and watch the color change back as the acid meets the base. (A taste of lemon juice is fine: it's food. Taste nothing else.)
Question: Which things in our house are acids, and which are bases? Table: thing / color / acid or base? New words: sour · slippery
After a rain, draw puddles, wet leaves or earthworms.
Fabre's chapter on salt: where salt comes from (the sea and salt mines) and why people have always needed it. Narrate: "How do people get salt?"

Look at salt grains under a magnifying glass: tiny cubes, like the crystals grown in Term 3. Then repeat Term 3's salt-water plate if it's sunny, to see the salt come back. History link: in the winter of 1805–1806, Lewis and Clark's men set up a camp on the Pacific coast and boiled seawater for weeks to make salt for the journey home.
Question: What shape is salt? Draw a magnified salt crystal. New words: salt · crystal · cube
Watch and draw one insect: a bee, a beetle or an ant. Label its head, body and legs.
Fabre's chapter on soap: how soap was made long ago from fat and ashes, and how it cleans. Narrate: "How does soap help clean greasy hands?"

(1) Pepper scatter: sprinkle ground pepper on a bowl of water. Touch the middle with a fingertip dipped in dish soap: the pepper rushes to the edges. (2) Oil and water: pour water and a little oil into a jar, close it and shake. They separate again. Add a drop of dish soap and shake: now they mix. Soap grabs onto grease so water can wash it away.
Question: How does soap help water clean? Draw the jar before and after the soap. New words: soap · grease
Draw the year tree in spring, with its new leaves or blossoms.

Parent explains: for most of history, colors for cloth came from plants, such as indigo for blue, madder for red and onion skins for yellow-brown. History Term 2 dyed cloth with onion skins; now try more colors. Narrate: "Where did people get colors for cloth before modern dyes?"

Parent at the stove: make two or three dye pots (onion skins, chopped beets, a spoonful of turmeric), each simmered in water. Dip strips of white cotton cloth in each and let them sit. Rinse and dry. Then drip a little cabbage juice (week 25) on a strip: does it change color? Fine Arts link: natural colors.
Question: What colors can plants make? Glue a small piece of each dyed strip into the notebook and label it. New words: dye · color
Find three flowers of different colors and draw them in color.
The child reads back the term's lab notebook pages and the read-aloud so far.
The child chooses a favorite demonstration from the term and does it again, explaining each step aloud to the family.
Below. Written, about 15 minutes.
Draw something that has grown since the start of the term.
1. Red cabbage juice that changes color to tell us about something is called an ___.
2. What color does vinegar turn cabbage juice?
3. What color does baking soda water turn it?
4. Is vinegar an acid or a base?
5. Is soap usually an acid or a base?
6. How can salt be made from seawater?
7. What shape are salt crystals?
8. Why does soap help clean greasy hands?
9. Name one plant that can make a dye.
10. Describe one demonstration from this term in 2–3 sentences.

1. Indicator · 2. Pink (or red) · 3. Green or blue · 4. An acid · 5. A base · 6. By letting the water evaporate, or by boiling it away · 7. Cubes · 8. It grabs onto grease so water can wash it away · 9. Any one: onion skins, beets, turmeric, indigo, madder · 10. Any clear description with what was done and what was seen.
Standard: 8 of 10. Below that, review the missed ideas at the start of Term 6.
The cabbage juice keeps in the refrigerator for a week. Make it once in week 25 and use it again in weeks 26 and 29.
Dyeing stains. Wear old clothes, cover the counter, and use rubber gloves for the beet pot.
Fabre is the parent's guide this term. Read his salt and soap chapters beforehand; his stories of how salt and soap were made long ago are worth retelling at the table.
Gather the term's materials before week 25
Begin The Mystery of the Periodic Table in week 25
Add "acid, base, indicator" to the Memory Work queue
Week 30: give the term check and record the score

terms.mastery: Standard: 8 of 10. Below that, review the missed ideas at the start of Term 6.

head: Big idea
All matter is made of elements, the simplest kinds of matter. The early chemists found them one by one.
rows: Elements around the house · oxygen and air · water is made of two elements · the chemists and the atom · year review · year-end demonstration
The Mystery of the Periodic Table (Wiker), continuing with the chapters on Boyle, Priestley, Lavoisier and Dalton · Fabre, The Secret of Everyday Things, the chapters on air and water, for the parent
Ten elements and their symbols: hydrogen H, helium He, carbon C, nitrogen N, oxygen O, aluminum Al, iron Fe, copper Cu, silver Ag, gold Au
Late spring: leaves in full, seeds and fruit forming, the year tree's last drawing

glance.text: How each week works. A: read and narrate. B: the demonstration, with a parent. C: the lab notebook page (the question, what we did, what we saw, new words). D: the nature journal.
Atoms are named, not explained (plan §1). This term introduces the word atom and the idea that everything is made of tiny pieces, as Dalton taught. How atoms work belongs to later grades.

History link. The chemists go on the History timeline: Boyle (1661), Priestley (1774, the same year as the First Continental Congress), Lavoisier (1783, the same year as the Treaty of Paris) and Dalton (1808).
Safety. The parent handles the 9-volt battery in week 33 and the candle in week 32.

blocks.text: Aluminum foil · a copper item (copper wire or a pot) · an iron nail · a silver spoon or coin, if the family has one · a pencil and charcoal (from a grill) · a candle, a clear jar and matches (parent only) · a 9-volt battery, a clear cup, water and baking soda (parent) · a helium balloon, if one is easy to get · index cards for the element symbols

The Mystery of the Periodic Table, continuing from Term 5. Parent explains: an element is the simplest kind of matter. It can't be broken down into anything simpler. Gold, iron and oxygen are elements; water and salt are not (they're made of elements joined together). Narrate: "What is an element?"

Element hunt: find elements around the house. Aluminum (foil), copper (wire or a pot), iron (a nail), silver (a spoon or coin, if you have one). Carbon is in pencil "lead", which is really graphite, a form of carbon, and in charcoal. Rub a pencil and a piece of charcoal on paper and compare.
Question: Which elements can we find at home? List each with where you found it and its symbol. New words: element · metal · symbol
Draw the year tree in full leaf.

The Mystery of the Periodic Table, the chapters on Joseph Priestley and Antoine Lavoisier: Priestley found a gas that made flames burn brighter, and Lavoisier named it oxygen and showed that burning needs it. Narrate: "What did Priestley discover?"
Parent only: repeat Term 4's candle under a jar, and time how long the flame lasts. Then try a bigger jar: does the flame last longer? A bigger jar holds more air, and so more oxygen.
Question: Does a bigger jar keep the candle burning longer? Record the times. New words: oxygen · nitrogen (most of the air is nitrogen; about a fifth is oxygen)
Plants give off oxygen. Draw a plant with its leaves, and label the leaves "give off oxygen".

weeks.title: Water is made of two elements

blocks.text: The Mystery of the Periodic Table, on Lavoisier and water: water is made of two elements, hydrogen and oxygen, joined together. Narrate: "What two elements make water?"

Parent only: stir a spoonful of baking soda into a clear cup of water. Dip both terminals of a 9-volt battery into the water, without letting them touch each other. Tiny bubbles rise from both terminals: the electricity is splitting a little of the water into hydrogen and oxygen gas. Watch for a minute, then take the battery out.
Question: Can water be split into the elements it's made of? Draw the battery with its bubbles. New words: hydrogen · water
Look for seeds forming on a plant or tree. Draw them.

The Mystery of the Periodic Table, on Robert Boyle and John Dalton. Boyle taught that elements are the simplest substances. Dalton taught that all matter is made of tiny pieces called atoms, too small to see, and that each element has its own kind. Narrate: "What did Dalton say everything is made of?"

How small? Cut a strip of paper in half, then cut one half in half again, and again, as many times as you can. You'll stop long before you reach an atom: there are more atoms in a grain of salt than grains of sand on a beach. Then make element cards: the ten elements, each with its symbol on one side and its name on the other.
Question: How small can we cut something? Record how many cuts you made. Copy the ten elements and symbols. New words: atom
Add the four chemists to the History timeline with their dates: Boyle 1661, Priestley 1774, Lavoisier 1783, Dalton 1808. (This week's journal is a timeline page.)
The child reads back the year's lab notebook, one term a day, and picks a favorite demonstration from each term.
The child chooses one demonstration from the year to present in week 36 and practices it: the materials, the steps, what to watch for and what it shows.
Write the plan for the week 36 demonstration: question, materials, steps, what we expect to see.
Draw the year tree one last time, and lay all the year's tree drawings side by side.
The child names the ten elements from their symbols, using the element cards.
The child presents their chosen demonstration to the family or co-op: explaining what they're doing, what to watch, and what it shows (plan §7).
Below. Written, about 15 minutes.
A free choice: the child's favorite thing to draw outdoors. File the year's journal in the portfolio.
1. What is an element?
2. Name two metal elements.
3. Pencil "lead" is really a form of which element?
4. Which gas in the air is needed for burning?
5. Water is made of hydrogen and ___.
6. What is the symbol for gold?
7. What is the symbol for oxygen?
8. Who taught that all matter is made of tiny atoms?
9. Who named oxygen and showed that water is made of two elements?
10. Describe one demonstration from this term in 2–3 sentences.

1. The simplest kind of matter; it can't be broken down into anything simpler · 2. Any two: iron, copper, aluminum, silver, gold · 3. Carbon · 4. Oxygen · 5. Oxygen · 6. Au · 7. O · 8. John Dalton · 9. Antoine Lavoisier · 10. Any clear description with what was done and what was seen.
Standard: 8 of 10.

T1 ___ · T2 ___ · T3 ___ · T4 ___ · T5 ___ · T6 ___ (each of 10)

Complete for the year: yes / mostly

blocks.text: Grade 4 is physics. Next year's science, physics and technology, builds on this year's matter and changes. The lab notebook habit matters more than any single fact.
The battery demonstration is brief: one minute is enough to see the bubbles. Don't let the terminals touch, and don't leave the battery in the water.
The year-end demonstration is the child's own work. Help gather materials; let them do the explaining.
Gather the term's materials before week 31
Make the ten element cards in week 34; add them to the Memory Work queue
Add the four chemists to the History timeline in week 34
Week 36: hear the demonstration, give the term check, complete the year-end record and file the notebooks
